The LRO launched in 2009. For almost two decades, the orbiter has been collecting data on the moon’s topography, surface composition, temperature and radiation environment. According to Powell and colleagues, the chillier temperature is due to the regolith—moon dirt—getting fluffed up by the impact, reducing the material’s density and ability to retain heat.

Additionally, Wagner and colleagues found that ejected material disturbed the surface more than 75 miles from the crater. That, combined with the expanse of the relatively frigid area, demonstrates the far-reaching effects of incoming space rocks, which have implications for people and technology that might roam that terrain.

“If we’re trying to send rovers or astronauts or build things on the moon, we want to understand the properties of the surface,” Powell tells New Scientist’s Leah Crane. The opportunity to study the development and transformation of a large new crater is a fantastic way to do that from a distance, according to the outlet.

NASA is forging ahead with its plan to establish an enduring human presence on the moon, so scientists need to calculate the risk of debris from impacts hitting the agency’s future moon base, Mark Robinson, who co-authored the study Wagner worked on and is part of LRO’s camera team at Intuitive Machines, tells the Associated Press’ Marcia Dunn.
Quick fact: Another notable new crater
On August 5, the moon gained another new divot, but this one wasn’t made by a natural phenomenon. It was struck by a stray SpaceX rocket part.

“Collisions are a pervasive physical process during planet formation and evolution,” Sarah T. Stewart, a planetary scientist at Arizona State University who didn’t participate in either study, told Universe Today’s Laurence Tognetti in 2024. “They provide key insights into planetary dynamics, subsurface composition and internal structure.”

Unlike Earth, whose atmosphere slows and burns up most incoming space rocks, the moon lacks an envelope of gases and is vulnerable to all impactors. It is therefore covered in pockmarks, but most are ancient and have been altered by other impacts and the harsh environment of space. Meanwhile, newer craters are typically too small to study with spacecraft images.
That means the 2024 impact that created McGetchin crater “constitutes a statistically rare, effectively once-in-a-lifetime observation,” Robinson, Wagner and colleagues write in their study.
